notes: ⚠ Ten verdict rows depend on creating symbolic links on Windows: `TestReadlink` with its six symlink subtests (`symlink_dir_drive_absolute`, `symlink_dir_volume_absolute`, `symlink_dir_volume_relative`, `symlink_file_drive_absolute`, `symlink_file_volume_absolute`, `symlink_file_volume_relative`), and `TestOpenFileCreateExclDanglingSymlink` with its `InRoot` and `NoRoot` subtests. They need unprivileged symbolic-link creation, which Windows grants under Developer Mode or to a holder of `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege`. On a host with it, all ten run and pass on both runtimes (measured 2026-10-01). On a host without it, all ten fail on both runtimes, agreeing name for name, so they count as matched without exercising the code under test; that is why a bank of this row states its host context.

disclosures.name: TestUTF16Alloc
disclosures.reason: exact-count AllocsPerRun asserts (want 1, for syscall.UTF16ToString and syscall.UTF16FromString): each leg allocates ONE object in Go and more than one in the managed model, so the exact count cannot agree. Go's `syscall.UTF16ToString([]uint16{'a','b','c'})` allocates only the returned string - escape analysis keeps the three-element array literal in the caller's frame - where the converted path must heap-allocate that array and its slice descriptor before the produced @string is counted at all; UTF16FromString is the mirror. That is this class's definition exactly: Go's compiler stack-allocates the value where .NET must heap-allocate it. The per-object split is NOT decomposed here - only the totals are measured. READINGS, recorded as a MOVE rather than a replacement, because this number is not stable and an entry that claims it is stops the next reader re-measuring. 2026-08-29 census: 4 allocs per run, 1,400 bytes. 2026-09-01 at master bfc63d487: 4 allocs per run, 20 go2cs-runtime allocations / 1,440 bytes over 5 runs. 2026-09-06 at the train-30 assembly head 9c33b95c0, Release with tiering off, read from the run's own unit note: 2 allocs per run, 10 go2cs-runtime allocations / 640 bytes over 5 runs - so the count HALVED and the bytes with it. The direction is TOWARD the want of 1, which is the opposite of drift. What caused the halving is NOT attributed here: something between 2026-09-01 and that head did it, it has not been measured, and a plausible cause written into a disclosure is read as established by whoever quotes it next. If a later reading reaches the want the assertion passes and this entry RETIRES - and that retirement should record whether the equality was EARNED or whether the managed floor simply sits there, since a nonzero-byte result reports at least 1 by construction. PRIOR REASON RETIRED, per the coordinator ruling of 2026-08-29: this entry used to argue a UNITS mismatch - that the shim was byte-derived and reported bytes where Go reports mallocs, citing 432 and 128 - and that argument no longer describes the instrument. The host now reports a genuine allocation COUNT from golib's own allocation sites, the structural mirror of Go's runtime.MemStats.Mallocs (a LOWER BOUND on the true object count, since C#-compiler and BCL allocations sit outside it), so the comparison is same-units and the row is disclosed on the allocation PROFILE instead. The deliberate asymmetry with os's TestWriteStringAlloc still stands and is now the load-bearing distinction rather than a units accident: that test bounds allocations at ZERO, a bound a correct implementation could in principle meet, so under ruling #1 of 2026-08-02 it is NOT disclosed and remains a real divergence and an open architectural arc. See the AllocsPerRun entry in docs/ConversionStrategies-Reference.md. RELABEL 2026-09-23 (C1, as ruled at ledger 2026-09-23 03:37 O5): alloc-profile -> deferred. The string-byte-window record could not reach this site until its §6 amendment (§2 covers only the unsafe.Slice direction).

disclosures.name: TestWriteStringAlloc
disclosures.reason: exact-count AllocsPerRun assert: os.File.WriteString must allocate ZERO objects per run, and the converted path allocates four. DEFERRED rather than alloc-count-semantics, and the discriminator is the run's own unit note rather than a source read: the host reports `counted 400 go2cs-runtime object allocations (42,400 bytes) over 100 run(s)`, so the counter SAW the allocations and the figure is an allocation COUNT per run - same units as Go's, which is exactly the case the deferred class exists for. It carries no `floor`: nothing in the CLR's object model requires an allocation to write a string through a file descriptor, so the whole excess is reducible bridge work rather than a structural minimum, and a floor claim here would be one the census could not falsify. SCOPE OF THE MEASUREMENT: Release with tiering off, the configuration of record, read back from the comparison record's own environment block rather than assumed; no other configuration was run and none is claimed. The reading was re-measured at the train-30 drop after a seat was removed from that assembly - the row's bank condition - and did not move: four per run at 9c33b95c0 and at 8693aa5ba alike, with the landing tree verified to differ from the measured tree in two behavioral golden files and nothing under src/core.
disclosures.reading: 4 per run - 400 go2cs-runtime object allocations (42,400 bytes) counted over 100 runs at 3737ed9a6, Release with tiering off. LINUX (WSL arm, Release with tiering off, 2026-09-27, os -tests at 448efc4f0b + the TRAIN E/F os seats): the same 4 per run - 400 counted (32,800 bytes) - reported on the COUNT path (the counter saw the allocations), so the same meter as the windows reading and the same label; the bytes are per-platform and 82 bytes per counted object is again well above a golib box, so the plan's note that part of the target sits outside golib's counter holds on linux too
disclosures.plan: the os want-zero arc, whose mechanism family is the zh-box capability set: docs/phase4/DESIGN-zh-box-three-capabilities.md carries the increments (C0 the contract, then I1/I3/I4/I5), and docs/phase4/DESIGN-string-byte-window.md is candidate C - the converter-side recognition of unsafe.Slice(unsafe.StringData(s), len(s)) that removes the element box at os/file.go:300, this row's own site. Each increment carries its own acceptance and the entry retires when the reading reaches its want. That retirement is SOUND ON THIS METER, and the reason is worth recording because it is not obvious: golib own allocation counter is blind to boxing (R measured 24 bytes charged as zero objects, 2026-09-06), so a count of zero could in principle hide real allocation - but testing.AllocsPerRun never reports that zero. It returns 0.0 only on the `allocated == 0` early return, i.e. only when the BYTE total is zero; when bytes are nonzero and the counter saw nothing it falls back to the byte figure floored at 1, precisely so a real allocation cannot become a passing assert. So a reading of 0 already implies zero bytes, boxes included, and the want is reachable only by genuinely allocating nothing. THE TARGET IS BYTES, AND OBJECT-COUNT WORK ALONE CAN NEVER REACH IT (coordinator ruling 2026-09-06, from R's correction of its own census). The pass condition is `allocated == 0`; the counted objects only decide which UNIT the helper reports. So driving golib's counted objects to zero while bytes remain nonzero does not retire this entry - it moves the row from the count branch to the BYTE branch, where it still fails with a figure in a different unit that reads exactly like the fix not working. This row's own numbers say that is not hypothetical: 400 counted objects against 42,400 bytes over 100 runs is 106 bytes per counted object, far more than a golib box costs, so well over a hundred bytes per run sit OUTSIDE golib's counter - CLR boxing, compiler-emitted closures and BCL internals, which the plan's own instrument cannot see. The arc's target is therefore partly invisible to the census that sizes it, and the increment that claims this row must show the BYTE figure reaching zero rather than the object count.

disclosures.name: TestRemoveAllNoFcntl
disclosures.reason: the test runs its own binary under `strace -f -e fcntl` to remove 100 directories and asserts fewer than 100 fcntl calls, reasoning that RemoveAll must not fcntl once per directory; strace -f counts EVERY fcntl the child PROCESS makes, and the converted child is a CLR-hosted executable. Measured on the WSL arm (2026-09-26/27): inside the RemoveAll window the child makes ZERO fcntl calls (99 openat, 198 getdents64, 300 unlinkat, 101 close - Go's descriptor-relative removal exactly), while all 309-312 counted calls come from the .NET runtime opening its ~153 managed assembly files at startup, each an openat followed by F_SETFD and F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC; the count is the same for the published single-file host and for `dotnet os.tests.dll` (312 and 312), so it is a property of loading managed assemblies from files, not of the packaging. The property the test guards holds; what cannot meet its budget is the deployment shape. The count assertion is the test's only failure text besides t.Fatal on setup errors, which this signature does not match. Retires under a deployment that loads no managed assembly files at startup (e.g. a Native AOT host) - unmeasured, named so a future shape change is checked against it.
